cards.scenario: Detect running EC2 with unapproved AMI without blocking deployments; send compliance notifications.
cards.ok: AWS Config managed rule approved-amis-by-id + SNS notification.
cards.bad: SCP and IAM policy denying launches of unapproved AMIs.
cards.why: SCP/IAM would block launches, which is forbidden. Config evaluates after deployment.

cards.scenario: AD corporate login to AWS, federate third-party apps, LEAST management overhead.
cards.ok: IAM Identity Center with Organizations + two-way forest trust to AWS Managed Microsoft AD.
cards.bad: AD FS with SAML 2.0 and Regex group mapping.
cards.why: Identity Center needs two-way trust and has third-party app integration; AD FS adds management.

cards.scenario: Most secure access for third-party auditor to your AWS resources.
cards.ok: Cross-account IAM role with only the actions the audit needs.
cards.bad: Cross-account IAM role with full unrestricted access.
cards.why: Role gives temporary credentials; least privilege limits the auditor to required actions only.

cards.scenario: Which IAM policies control EC2 role access to S3 files (select two).
cards.ok: Permissions policy allowing S3 access + trust policy letting EC2 service assume role.
cards.bad: Trust policy letting the NodeJS application access S3 files.
cards.why: Trust policy only defines who may assume the role; EC2 is the principal. Permissions policy grants S3 access.

cards.scenario: Mobile tax app users access S3 directly; secure authentication, temporary access.
cards.ok: IAM role; generate temporary credentials with STS AssumeRole when user uses the app.
cards.bad: Create an IAM user and store its access keys in the mobile app.
cards.why: Never embed long-term credentials in an app; use roles and temporary STS credentials.

cards.scenario: SCP allows EC2 and S3 yet IAM user gets denied creating bucket.
cards.ok: IAM user lacks IAM policy explicitly granting EC2 or S3 actions.
cards.bad: Attach the SCP manually to each account in the OU.
cards.why: SCPs only limit permissions, never grant them. SCP on an OU is inherited automatically.

cards.scenario: AD login to S3, each user restricted to own folder (select two).
cards.ok: IAM policy limiting user-specific S3 folders + federation proxy/custom IdP with STS temporary tokens and IAM role.
cards.bad: IAM user per corporate user with folder-restricting IAM policy.
cards.why: Federation gives SSO via temporary STS tokens; per-user IAM users defeat single sign-on.

cards.scenario: Management role gets Access Denied on Marketing S3 bucket with custom KMS key.
cards.ok: Role policy (S3 read + KMS decrypt), bucket policy for Management account, KMS key policy for role.
cards.bad: Bucket policy with Principal set to the Marketing account ID.
cards.why: Cross-account needs both sides: role policy, bucket policy for Management, and KMS key policy decrypt.

cards.scenario: Enforce predefined tags before anyone launches EC2 instances, simplest way.
cards.ok: Organizations OUs + SCP using ForAllValues and aws:TagKeys condition, applied to OU.
cards.bad: IAM policy per member account with aws:TagKeys condition.
cards.why: An SCP on the OU cascades to all member accounts; per-account IAM policies are not simplest.

cards.scenario: Social-login voting site absorbing huge surges, cost-effective.
cards.ok: CloudFront + ALB + Auto Scaling EC2, Cognito auth, SQS queue, DynamoDB results.
cards.bad: Servers authenticate users with IAM, store votes in RDS.
cards.why: Cognito supports social sign-in at scale; SQS buffers surges and DynamoDB scales automatically.

cards.scenario: EC2 instances reach DynamoDB from CloudFormation template without exposing API credentials.
cards.ok: IAM role referenced in AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile for application instances.
cards.bad: IAM role referenced via AWS::IAM::InstanceRoleName property.
cards.why: Instances use roles through an instance profile; no access keys exposed.

cards.scenario: ERP reachable by remote managers over Internet, not public; minimize cost.
cards.ok: SSL VPN in public subnet; ERP servers in private subnet.
cards.bad: IPsec VPN with app servers in a public subnet.
cards.why: App servers in public subnet become Internet-reachable. Private subnet behind SSL VPN stays hidden.

cards.scenario: Remote-employee Client VPN reaching peered VPCs; cost-effective, minimal changes.
cards.ok: Client VPN endpoint in the main account's VPC, with route updates.
cards.bad: Client VPN installed in data center, with Transit Gateway replacing existing VPC peering.
cards.why: Install client on employee workstations; main account endpoint suffices with peering. Transit Gateway means needless reconfiguration.

cards.scenario: Central rule-based outbound filtering for 50+ accounts on Transit Gateway.
cards.ok: Dedicated egress VPC with NAT gateway and Network Firewall, connected to Transit Gateway.
cards.bad: Network Firewall deployed separately in each account.
cards.why: Central egress VPC via Transit Gateway gives one managed inspection point instead of per-account firewalls.

cards.scenario: Replace two Direct Connect links with more cost-effective hybrid connectivity.
cards.ok: Single Direct Connect plus AWS managed VPN as backup.
cards.bad: Single Direct Connect with built-in failover feature.
cards.why: Direct Connect has no built-in failover; VPN is cheaper backup path.

cards.scenario: Most secure RDS MySQL replication to on-premises read-only MySQL.
cards.ok: IPsec VPN to on-premises; RDS as replication source, mysqldump seed, replicate from read replica.
cards.bad: Claim RDS cannot replicate on-premises; replicate to an EC2 MySQL instead.
cards.why: RDS MySQL can replicate to on-premises over IPsec VPN, keeping data encrypted in transit.

cards.scenario: Low-latency, high-bandwidth link from Texas data center to VPCs in two Regions, cost-effective.
cards.ok: Direct Connect gateway associated with two virtual private gateways.
cards.bad: Separate Direct Connect connection to each Region's VPC.
cards.why: A Direct Connect gateway is global, reaching VPCs in multiple Regions over one connection.

cards.scenario: UDP game servers on AWS with Shield Advanced; pick two actions.
cards.ok: NLB with Elastic IP for UDP + NACL denying non-UDP traffic on load balancer subnets.
cards.bad: CloudFront distribution with the load balancer as origin.
cards.why: NLB handles UDP; ALB and CloudFront are HTTP/HTTPS only, and WAF cannot filter UDP.

cards.scenario: Block a known set of attacking IP ranges at the VPC.
cards.ok: Inbound network ACL with explicit deny rules for the attacking IPs.
cards.bad: Security Group with explicit deny rules for the attacking IPs.
cards.why: Security groups only allow; network ACLs support explicit deny rules.

cards.scenario: Block direct S3 URL downloads; users must use CloudFront.
cards.ok: CloudFront OAC with read permission on bucket, and remove everyone else's S3 read permission.
cards.bad: Signed URLs with OAC, but leaving others' S3 read permission in place.
cards.why: Direct S3 access stays open unless other read permissions are removed.

cards.scenario: Offload traffic from on-premises website fast, within 3 months, cost-effective.
cards.ok: CloudFront distribution with on-premises URL as origin and DNS offloaded to AWS.
cards.bad: Replicate the infrastructure on AWS with Route 53 weighted routing 50%.
cards.why: Replicating the whole stack takes too long; CloudFront can use an on-premises origin immediately.

cards.scenario: 20 GB forecast overwritten every 15 minutes; 1,500 users/second, 10x spikes, under 2 seconds.
cards.ok: EFS on EC2 ASG behind ELB, CloudFront origin ELB with 15-minute cache-control.
cards.bad: OpenSearch with Lambda behind API Gateway and 15-minute API cache.
cards.why: Lambda concurrency burst limits can't absorb spikes; EFS plus CloudFront caching serves quickly.

cards.scenario: Static assets return 404 though ALB is default CloudFront origin and OAC set.
cards.ok: Add separate S3 origin in CloudFront + path-pattern behavior routing static requests to it.
cards.bad: Add ALB path-based listener rule forwarding static requests to the S3 bucket.
cards.why: ALB cannot forward to S3; CloudFront needs an S3 origin plus path-pattern behavior.

cards.scenario: End-to-end HTTPS from viewers through CloudFront to ALB origin, custom domain.
cards.ok: Third-party CA cert imported to ACM on ALB; HTTPS Only; third-party cert in ACM or IAM for CloudFront.
cards.bad: Self-signed certificate on the ALB with HTTPS Only viewer policy.
cards.why: Origin ALB needs a trusted CA or ACM certificate; self-signed certificates are rejected.

cards.scenario: Stop third-party hotlinking of S3 photos and speed up loading.
cards.ok: Remove S3 public read; CloudFront with signed URLs with expiry.
cards.bad: CloudFront but block offending sites' IP addresses.
cards.why: Signed URLs restrict access to authorized users; CloudFront speeds delivery; IP blocking is ineffective.

cards.scenario: Python/TypeScript developers need loops, no new DSL, to keep using CloudFormation pipeline.
cards.ok: Define resources in Python/TypeScript with AWS CDK, synthesize CloudFormation, deploy via CodeBuild/CodePipeline.
cards.bad: Plain CloudFormation templates with Python snippets as EC2 user data.
cards.why: CDK uses familiar languages with loops and compiles to CloudFormation, fitting the existing pipeline.

cards.scenario: Automatically test CloudFormation templates from private GitHub before production.
cards.ok: CodePipeline from GitHub: change set + execute, plus CodeBuild stage running tests.
cards.bad: CodePipeline with CodeDeploy stage to create and execute the change set.
cards.why: CodeDeploy is unnecessary; CodeBuild runs test scripts to verify the new stack.

cards.scenario: Re-architect video service: reduce cost, drop third-party software, less management.
cards.ok: ECS Fargate web tier, Spot EC2 SQS workers, Rekognition, videos on S3.
cards.bad: S3 website hosting for the web app, with S3 events, SQS, Lambda and Rekognition.
cards.why: The app is dynamic; S3 static website hosting cannot do server-side processing.

cards.scenario: CI/CD from GitHub with scanning, test-failure alerts, feature toggles, lead developer approval.
cards.ok: CodeBuild tests/scans + EventBridge to SNS alerts + CDK feature manifest + manual approval stage.
cards.bad: Lambda function running unit tests and scans, notifying via SES approval email.
cards.why: Tests may exceed Lambda's 15 minutes; CodeBuild fits, and pipeline manual approval is simpler than SES.

cards.scenario: Automate deployment with fastest rollback to older version.
cards.ok: Two Elastic Beanstalk environments, blue/green by swapping URL, scripts via platform hooks.
cards.bad: SSM Automation runbook deploying to staging with automated tests, then production.
cards.why: Swapping the environment URL back is a fast rollback; runbook rollback is a separate process.

cards.scenario: Legacy app: hardcoded DB IPs, license tied to MAC address (select two).
cards.ok: Lambda updates DB IPs in Parameter Store + pool of licensed ENIs, license files in S3.
cards.bad: Base AMI from a licensed instance with configured database IPs.
cards.why: A new instance gets a new MAC address, invalidating the license; license files in S3 scale easily.

cards.scenario: Terminate one instance when cluster CPU is 15% or lower; cost-effective.
cards.ok: CloudWatch alarm with Auto Scaling scale-in policy removing one instance.
cards.bad: Scheduled actions in the Auto Scaling group.
cards.why: CPU load is unpredictable, so scheduled actions do not fit; the ASG has built-in dynamic scaling.

cards.scenario: Cheapest fast recovery from AZ outage; web servers run at 90% at peak.
cards.ok: Spot Fleet mixing On-Demand and Spot across multiple AZs behind an ALB.
cards.bad: Auto Scaling group of only On-Demand instances across multiple AZs behind ALB.
cards.why: Mixed fleet is cheaper than all On-Demand and avoids Spot-only reclaim risk to availability.

cards.scenario: Migrate site: more security, availability, lower latency, less maintenance overhead.
cards.ok: S3 static content behind CloudFront with WAF + EC2 Auto Scaling over two AZs with RDS Multi-AZ.
cards.bad: Self-managed MySQL master/slave cluster on EC2 across two AZs.
cards.why: Managed RDS Multi-AZ cuts maintenance and adds availability; CloudFront cuts latency, WAF blocks exploits.

cards.scenario: 24/7 highly available, fault-tolerant grocery site.
cards.ok: Three AZs with Auto Scaled EC2 behind ALB and RDS Multi-AZ.
cards.bad: Three AZs, ALB, one RDS instance with read replicas in two AZs.
cards.why: RDS Multi-AZ gives database failover; read replicas are for read scaling, not HA.

cards.scenario: Improve network performance between outside controller instance and placement group.
cards.ok: Stop the controller instance and move it into the existing placement group.
cards.bad: Terminate controller, stop all group instances, move controller in, restart all.
cards.why: Stopping and moving the instance suffices; no terminate or restarting group instances needed.

cards.scenario: Deploy resources across multiple Regions and accounts in an Organization.
cards.ok: CloudFormation StackSets orchestrated centrally via Organizations.
cards.bad: Control Tower as the orchestration layer for CloudFormation deployments.
cards.why: StackSets roll out stacks to many accounts and Regions with simplified permissions.

cards.scenario: Automate updating CloudFormation templates with latest AMI IDs.
cards.ok: SSM Parameter Store parameter type in template; call update-stack for new AMIs.
cards.bad: Systems Manager State Manager storing AMI IDs for the template.
cards.why: CloudFormation fetches AMI IDs referenced in Parameter Store; State Manager is not a parameter store.

cards.scenario: Slow answer submissions and slow image loads; most cost-effective, scalable.
cards.ok: SQS queue buffers submissions + CloudFront with S3 for static assets.
cards.bad: DynamoDB auto scaling at 100% target utilization, S3 only without CloudFront.
cards.why: Queue absorbs write spikes; CloudFront caches assets at edge. Auto scaling target utilization only allows 20-90%.

cards.scenario: Write-intensive donation site, unpredictable traffic spike; best solution.
cards.ok: DynamoDB with provisioned writes; SQS buffers writes for Auto Scaled EC2 consumers.
cards.bad: DynamoDB + CloudFront only, no write buffering.
cards.why: SQS buffers the burst; DynamoDB stores large data cheaply. CloudFront only caches, no buffering.

cards.scenario: Managed call center with scaling and intent recognition (select two).
cards.ok: Amazon Connect contact center + Amazon Lex bot for caller intent.
cards.bad: Kinesis stream with Amazon Comprehend for caller intent from voice.
cards.why: Lex does intent from speech; Comprehend only analyzes text, Rekognition is for images.

cards.scenario: Location alert within a minute for 10 million users across Asia.
cards.ok: Device location to SQS; ALB+ASG API reads DynamoDB offers; SNS mobile push.
cards.bad: Kinesis for location, then Lambda and SES for notifications.
cards.why: SNS mobile push delivers the alert; SES is email and cannot push to phones.

cards.scenario: 20,000 sensors, query one sensor for past week, delete data over eight weeks, cost-effective.
cards.ok: One table per week, sensor ID partition key + timestamp sort key.
cards.bad: Single table with sensor ID key and timestamp as hash key.
cards.why: Weekly tables allow dropping old data cheaply; single table grows huge and slows searches.

cards.scenario: Comments must appear in real-time on API Gateway/Lambda/DynamoDB app.
cards.ok: AWS AppSync GraphQL API with WebSocket subscriptions.
cards.bad: CloudFront with edge-optimized API caching of comment responses.
cards.why: Cached responses may be stale and not real-time; AppSync pushes updates over WebSockets.

cards.scenario: Stateful web app and Aurora must scale with unpredictable traffic.
cards.ok: Aurora Replica with Aurora Auto Scaling + ALB with sticky sessions in front of ASG.
cards.bad: Aurora Auto Scaling for the master database.
cards.why: Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas, not primary resizing. ALB suits stateful web layer; NLB unneeded.

cards.scenario: Cut RDS MySQL failover below 20 seconds, keep connections, queue writes (select three).
cards.ok: RDS Proxy + migrate to Aurora MySQL + Aurora Multi-AZ with replicas.
cards.bad: Keep RDS Multi-AZ with read replicas.
cards.why: Plain RDS failover can take up to 60 seconds, and replicas do not queue writes. Proxy + Aurora does.

cards.scenario: Orchestrate batch workflows with state management, failure reprocessing, concurrent operations.
cards.ok: Step Functions orchestrating batch workflows, monitored in the console.
cards.bad: Workflow state stored in RDS, with Lambda functions polling for changes.
cards.why: Step Functions manages workflow state natively; RDS polling adds overhead.

cards.scenario: Queue-driven file processing, 30 minutes each, peak in business hours; cost-effective.
cards.ok: SQS queue + EC2 Auto Scaling on queue length + processed files in S3.
cards.bad: SQS with Lambda processing, since each file takes 30 minutes.
cards.why: Lambda maximum runtime is 15 minutes, too short for 30-minute processing jobs.

cards.scenario: Migrate game REST API with API keys unchanged; scalable, low-latency session data.
cards.ok: Lambda logic behind API Gateway (API keys) + DynamoDB with auto scaling.
cards.bad: Lambda logic behind an ALB with DynamoDB.
cards.why: API Gateway natively supports API keys and request customization; ALB lacks that flexibility.

cards.scenario: Ingest sensor data in real time, ETL to warehouse, archive, live dashboard.
cards.ok: Data Firehose to S3, lifecycle to Glacier, EMR processing, load to Redshift.
cards.bad: Store raw data in S3 with Lake Formation, EMR ETL, then Redshift.
cards.why: Real-time collection points to Kinesis; Data Firehose delivers streaming data to S3 and Redshift.

cards.scenario: Month-end report spikes slow app; improve performance with LEAST availability impact.
cards.ok: Migrate EC2 database to RDS MySQL and add read replicas for month-end peak.
cards.bad: Swap EBS volumes to Provisioned IOPS at month end, revert afterward.
cards.why: RDS read replicas scale reads with little impact on availability; volume swaps risk disruption.

cards.scenario: Cut 45-minute photo metadata extraction time with Lambda.
cards.ok: Split Lambda per metadata type; Step Functions parallel workflow, second workflow per photo.
cards.bad: Step Functions parallel workflow fed by SQS queue of photos.
cards.why: Step Functions orchestrates parallel Lambdas directly; SQS in front adds an unneeded input layer.

cards.scenario: Slow reads in RDS database tier, instances already budget-optimized (select three).
cards.ok: Read replica per AZ + ElastiCache per AZ + sharding across multiple RDS MySQL instances.
cards.bad: Upgrade RDS MySQL to Provisioned IOPS.
cards.why: Replicas, caching and sharding scale reads; Provisioned IOPS or larger instances raise cost.

cards.scenario: Managed event buffer that scales, near-real-time dashboards, dynamic JSON schemas (select two).
cards.ok: Data Firehose buffering with Lambda transform + OpenSearch Service with OpenSearch Dashboards.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Streams ingest with Lambda transform.
cards.why: Firehose is managed and auto-scaling; OpenSearch handles semi-structured JSON with built-in dashboards.

cards.scenario: Database slow under 100,000 simultaneous requests; cost-effective fix (select two).
cards.ok: ElastiCache in-memory cache per AZ + RDS read replicas per AZ.
cards.bad: CloudFront distribution to fix latency.
cards.why: Slowness is in the database tier, so cache and read replicas help; CloudFront serves static content.

cards.scenario: 25 TB MySQL, 50 Mbps VPN, 3 weeks, LEAST downtime.
cards.ok: Export to Data Transfer Terminal, load into Aurora, then VPN replication until cutover.
cards.bad: DMS full load over the 50 Mbps VPN, then cut over.
cards.why: 25 TB cannot cross 50 Mbps VPN in 3 weeks; bulk export then replicate deltas.

cards.scenario: Convert VMware VMs into AMIs and migrate to AWS (select two).
cards.ok: Application Migration Service (MGN) + AWS Replication Agent on source servers.
cards.bad: CloudFormation template mirroring on-premises environment.
cards.why: MGN replicates source servers and converts them. CloudFormation builds new AWS AMIs, not your VMs.

cards.scenario: Migrate ~500 physical servers, separate staging/launch accounts, cross-region VPC creation.
cards.ok: AWS Transform MGN: replication agent on each machine, test, then cutover.
cards.bad: VM Import/Export converting servers to images and launching manually.
cards.why: VM Import/Export is manual and unscalable for hundreds of servers; MGN automates replication and cutover.

cards.scenario: Cross-region DR: RTO under 2 hours, RPO 10 minutes after DB loss.
cards.ok: Hourly backups to S3 with Cross-Region Replication + transaction logs every 5 minutes.
cards.bad: Synchronous source-replica replication between two Availability Zones.
cards.why: Two AZs do not protect against region-wide outage; backup logs replicated cross-region meet RPO/RTO.

cards.scenario: Redesign for media-file durability and cost-efficiency; replication job no longer scales.
cards.ok: Media files in S3 as CloudFront origin; ELB + Auto Scaling web servers; Cost Explorer + Trusted Advisor.
cards.bad: Media files on EFS mounted on Storage Optimized instances behind CloudFront.
cards.why: S3 is durable and cheaper for media; CloudFront origin plus Cost Explorer and Trusted Advisor monitor cost.

cards.scenario: Move 1 TB over 50-Mbps link in weekend window, most cost-effective.
cards.ok: S3 sync a week early, then a final delta sync on Friday.
cards.bad: Single S3 multipart upload Saturday morning through Sunday evening.
cards.why: sync uploads only deltas, so the Friday final sync takes a fraction of the time.

cards.scenario: Cut costly 120GB PIOPS EBS cost without hurting performance or durability.
cards.ok: Shared EFS mounted on all instances using Provisioned Throughput mode.
cards.bad: gp2 EBS volumes sized 1 TB for 3000 IOPS.
cards.why: EFS Provisioned Throughput sets throughput independent of size; Max I/O mode adds metadata latency.

cards.scenario: Archive huge files, 24-hour retrieval, searchable by metadata, cheapest.
cards.ok: Compress each data set into one Glacier archive; keep archive ID + metadata in DynamoDB.
cards.bad: Store individual compressed files in S3, metadata in a separate S3 bucket.
cards.why: Compressing lowers cost and Glacier search is slow, so metadata and archive ID go in DynamoDB.

cards.scenario: Migrate IBM WebSphere, MQ and Db2 cheaply with better availability.
cards.ok: DMS + SCT to Aurora, WebSphere on ASG behind ELB, IBM MQ re-platformed to Amazon MQ.
cards.bad: App Migration Service re-hosting WebSphere and Db2 on EC2, MQ to SQS Standard.
cards.why: Aurora and Amazon MQ are managed and available; SQS is not a drop-in for IBM MQ.

cards.scenario: Redshift with RPO 24 hours, RTO 1 hour, must survive Region outage.
cards.ok: Automatic snapshots with cross-region snapshot copy to the DR Region.
cards.bad: Redshift replication to a secondary-Region cluster, switch DNS on failure.
cards.why: Redshift does not replicate clusters across Regions; cross-region snapshot copy meets the RPO.

cards.scenario: Secure document store with versions and API-driven rollback for customer apps.
cards.ok: Amazon WorkDocs with access management, version control, built-in encryption, Content Manager integration.
cards.bad: S3 Versioning with client-side encryption and shared encryption keys.
cards.why: WorkDocs provides versioning and encryption built in; sharing encryption keys with customers is insecure.

cards.scenario: Auto-remove permissions of new IAM users and notify security team (select three).
cards.ok: EventBridge rule on CloudTrail CreateUser + Step Functions removes permissions + SNS topic notifies.
cards.bad: CloudTrail event filter sending to SNS + EventBridge invoking Fargate task.
cards.why: CloudTrail filters cannot notify SNS; EventBridge cannot directly invoke Fargate.

cards.scenario: Public S3 object must notify compliance immediately and auto-remediate.
cards.ok: CloudTrail object-level logging + EventBridge rule: SNS notify + Lambda sets object private.
cards.bad: Hourly scheduled EventBridge/Lambda check invoking SSM Automation.
cards.why: Hourly scan delays notification; requirement is as soon as created. Event-driven rule is immediate.

cards.scenario: Dev team can log into EC2 but must not access Security team's SSL certificate.
cards.ok: Store cert in IAM/ACM with Security-only IAM policy; terminate SSL on ALB.
cards.bad: Fetch read-only certificate copy from CloudHSM at EC2 boot.
cards.why: Terminate SSL at the ALB with certificate in IAM or ACM, controlling access by IAM policy.

cards.scenario: Auto-generated DB password stored securely, rotated every 90 days, least overhead.
cards.ok: Secrets Manager secret with managed rotation; AutomaticallyAfterDays in RotationRules.
cards.bad: Secrets Manager secret rotated by custom Lambda on EventBridge schedule.
cards.why: Secrets Manager managed rotation is built in; custom Lambda and scheduling add overhead.

cards.scenario: Find minimum permissions per Lambda role with LEAST effort (select two).
cards.ok: CloudTrail trail capturing S3/DynamoDB events + IAM Access Analyzer generating policy from CloudTrail logs.
cards.bad: Audit Manager continuous audit to hand-write restrictive policies.
cards.why: Access Analyzer builds a least-privilege policy template from CloudTrail activity automatically.

cards.scenario: Harden web app: stop SQLi/DDoS while keeping high availability and security.
cards.ok: ALB, Session Manager instead of SSH, RDS Multi-AZ, CloudFront with WAF, Shield Advanced.
cards.bad: Same design with RDS Single-AZ, WAF but without Shield Advanced.
cards.why: WAF counters SQL injection, Multi-AZ gives HA, Session Manager removes SSH, Shield Advanced adds DDoS protection.

cards.scenario: Lower DynamoDB cost for sleep-tracking app with daily 9 AM scan (select two).
cards.ok: Reserved capacity for DynamoDB + drop previous day's table after export, create a new daily table.
cards.bad: ElastiCache in front of DynamoDB to cache reads and writes.
cards.why: ElastiCache adds its own cost and saves less than reserved capacity and dropping old tables.

cards.scenario: RIs bought in PROD (us-west-2a); which member account gets the discount?
cards.ok: Only DEV, whose instances match the RI in us-west-2a.
cards.bad: Both DEV and UAT, since instance types match.
cards.why: RI pricing needs matching AZ too; UAT runs in us-west-1a so only DEV benefits.

cards.scenario: Auto-recover unreachable EC2 instances (network, RDP, firewall issues).
cards.ok: EC2Rescue run through Systems Manager Automation with AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Rescue.
cards.bad: EC2Rescue triggered by Lambda and a custom script.
cards.why: Automation document AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Rescue runs EC2Rescue automatically without custom code.
